The foundational concept of an 'event' serves as the core building block for probabilistic reasoning. In measure-theoretic probability, events are elements of a σ-algebra over a sample space Ω, enabling rigorous treatment of both discrete and continuous random phenomena. Each event E ⊆ Ω represents a collection of possible outcomes. For finite experiments like rolling a die, the power set of outcomes yields all admissible events. This structure supports the definition of probability measures P(E), which assign numerical values to events according to Kolmogorov's axioms. The use of set theory allows for complex event construction via unions, intersections, and complements, forming the basis for conditional probabilities and independence. When extended to infinite sample spaces, additional technical conditions ensure that probabilities remain well-defined. These primitives enable formal modeling of uncertainty in decision-making frameworks within GSI and GSE.
